exercises.title: Nico learns German: Could you please say that again?
texts:
Julia: Hallo, #p#?
Lennard: #p#.
Julia: Lennard? Bitte buchstabiere das.
Lennard: L-E-N-N-A-R-D.
Julia: Noch einmal bitte.
Lennard: #p#.
Julia: Ah ja. Danke.
Bring die Wörter und Sätze in die richtige Reihenfolge.

Herr Lübken: Hallo, wie ist Ihr Name?
Sophie: Mein Name ist Sophie Meier.
Herr Lübken: Sophie Meier? #p#.
Sophie: S-O-P-H-I-E M-E-I-E-R.

exercises.title: Nico learns German: What is your name?
texts: Careful! You only ask "Wie ist dein Name?" in informal situations. In formal situations, the question would be "Wie ist Ihr Name?".

Info: If you don't know how to write something, you can ask „Wie schreibt man das?“, „Bitte buchstabiere das!“ or „Bitte buchstabieren Sie das!“ If someone is speaking too quickly, you can say „Langsam, bitte!“ or „Noch einmal, bitte!“.

exercises.title: Nico learns the German alphabet
texts: F - G - H - I - J - K
L - M - N - O - P - Q
R – S – T – U – V – W
Careful! "Ä", "Ö" and "Ü" are the three letters in German with umlauts. "ß" is a special character in German. It only occurs in the middle and at the end of a word.

exercises.title: Spelling names
texts: Info: If you don't know how to write something, you can ask „Wie schreibt man das?“.

exercises.title: Understanding abbreviations
texts: New words: "PKW" (or "Pkw") is an abbreviation for "Personenkraftwagen" and refers to (passenger) cars. "LKW" (or "Lkw") stands for "Lastkraftwagen" (truck).
New words: The abbreviation "AGB" stands for "Allgemeine Geschäftsbedingungen" (general terms and conditions). "ABC" refers to the alphabet.
New words: "USA" and "USB" are English abbreviations. They stand for the English terms "United States of America" and "Universal Serial Bus", but are pronounced as if they were German abbreviations.
New words: The German abbreviation "DNA" corresponds to the abbreviation DNA. "DRK" stands for "Deutsches Rotes Kreuz" (the German Red Cross).

pages.title: How's it going?
texts:
The question "Wie geht es dir?" ("How are you?" – informal) or "Wie geht es Ihnen?" ("How are you?" – formal) often comes immediately after a greeting. It is a standard part of the conversation, as it is considered polite to ask someone how they are doing or feeling. But be careful: sometimes people are not really interested in the answer. In a conversation with someone you don't know that well, your answer should be very brief, for example, "Danke, gut" ("Very well, thanks)".
But if a friend asks you the question, you may respond honestly and in detail, since that person really wants to know how you are.

lines: Welcome to A1! | Von A bis Z
Lisa and Emma hear from Nico why he has come to Germany, and they give
him a ride into town. In the car, Emma arranges alphabet cookies to form
her name and teaches Nico how to introduce himself in German.
Nicht schlecht! Du willst zu deiner Tante? Zu Yara? Hast du die Adresse? Adresse:
Die kenn ich nicht … Komm, wir helfen dir!
Mein Name ist Emma! Und das ist meine Tante.
Nein, Lisa ist nicht meine Mama. Sie ist meine Tante. Meine Mama ... fliegt nach
bitte – here you go; please; if you please
der Buchstabe, die Buchstaben – letter (of the alphabet)
Bitte buchstabiere das. – Could you please spell that?
Bitte buchstabieren Sie das. – Could you please spell that?
fliegen – to fly; to fly in an airplane
die Hausnummer, die Hausnummern – street number
die Mama, die Mamas – mom; mother
Mein Name ist ... – My name is ...
Wie ist dein Name? – What is your name? (informal)
Wie ist Ihr Name? – What is your name? (formal)
die Straße, die Straßen – street; road
etwas suchen – to search for something; to look for something
Wie schreibt man das? – How do you write/spell that?
